hints: Compare M and R. M has one C=C bond and R has two C-OH groups on adjacent carbons, so think which mild oxidising agent adds two OH groups across a double bond.
walkthrough:
See what has been added across the double bond**
Look closely at M, cyclohexene, and R, cyclohexane-1,2-diol. The C=C has gone and two OH groups have appeared on neighbouring carbons. This is hydroxylation, a mild oxidation where oxygen and water add across the double bond, not full cleavage.

hints: For step 1, M to dibromide Q adds two Br atoms across the C=C, recall the standard reagent for bromination without substitution.
For step 2, two C-Br bonds in Q become two C-OH bonds in R, recall the aqueous alkaline reagent that substitutes Br by OH.
walkthrough:
Make the dibromoalkane Q**
M to Q adds one Br to each carbon of the double bond to give 1,2-dibromocyclohexane. The clean way to do this is $\text{Br}_{2}$ in the dark at room temperature. Darkness matters because UV light would cause free radical substitution of the alkane C-H bonds instead.

Replace Br by OH to make the diol R**
Q to R replaces both $\text{C-Br}$ bonds with $\text{C-OH}$ bonds. That is nucleophilic substitution by $\text{OH}^{-}$. Use $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ with heat so hydroxide ions are available in high concentration and both bromines are hydrolysed.

Final answer: step 1: $\text{Br}_{2}$ in the dark (in an inert solvent)
step 2: $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ with heat

hints: Think about how the electron rich C=C attacks the reagent in step 1 and what type of species $\text{Br}_{2}$ acts as.
walkthrough:
Recognise attack by the pi bond on an electrophile**
In step 1 the $\pi$ electrons of cyclohexene attack a slightly positive Br in $\text{Br}_{2}$. The alkene donates a pair of electrons to an electrophile and then a bromide ion adds to the carbocation intermediate. That two stage addition to a C=C is electrophilic addition.

hints: List the bonds present in both Q and R. Both contain cyclohexane C-H and C-C bonds, but only R contains O-H.
Use Table 5.1 for absorptions above $1500 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. Match the sharp peak near $2950 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and the broad peak near $3600 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ to the correct bonds.
walkthrough:
Find a peak common to both Q and R**
Q is 1,2-dibromocyclohexane and R is cyclohexane-1,2-diol. Both have lots of alkane $\text{C-H}$ bonds in the ring. In Fig. 5.3 there is a strong sharp absorption at about $2950 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. Table 5.1 shows $\text{C-H}$ (alkane) at 2850 to 2950 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. Label this F.

Find a peak unique to the diol**
Only R has hydroxy groups, so only R shows an $\text{O-H}$ stretch. In Fig. 5.3 there is a broad strong absorption at about $3600 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. Table 5.1 shows hydroxy $\text{O-H}$ at 3200 to 3650 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. Label this G. Q has no O-H so this peak is absent in Q.

Final answer: F at about 2850 to 2950 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ corresponds to $\text{C-H}$ (alkane), present in both Q and R.
G at about 3200 to 3650 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ corresponds to $\text{O-H}$ in hydroxy / alcohol, present in R but not in Q.

hints: $\text{CN}^{-}$ from KCN replaces $\text{Br}^{-}$ by nucleophilic substitution, consider how many C-Br bonds are replaced and what group replaces each.
walkthrough:
Substitute both Br atoms by CN**
$\text{KCN}$ in ethanol provides $\text{CN}^{-}$ which is a strong nucleophile. Each $\text{C-Br}$ undergoes nucleophilic substitution to $\text{C-C}\equiv\text{N}$. Since Q has two adjacent $\text{C-Br}$ bonds, W has two adjacent $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ groups on the cyclohexane ring.
Final answer: W is 1,2-dicyanocyclohexane: cyclohexane ring with $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ groups on two adjacent carbons.

hints: Heating a nitrile with $\text{HCl(aq)}$ gives a carboxylic acid plus nitrogen as an inorganic ion, think what $\text{NH}_{3}$ becomes in strong acid.
walkthrough:
Track the nitrogen from nitrile to ammonium**
Acid hydrolysis converts each $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ to $\text{-COOH}$ plus $\text{NH}_{3}$. In excess $\text{HCl(aq)}$ the ammonia is immediately protonated to $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$. With $\text{Cl}^{-}$ present the inorganic product is $\text{NH}_{4}\text{Cl}$.

hints: Compare formulas of X, $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{4}$, and Y, $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{16}\text{O}_{2}$, and count O atoms lost as water to balance H from Z.
walkthrough:
Balance reduction of two COOH to two CH2OH**
X is a dicarboxylic acid, $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{4}$, and Y is the corresponding diol, $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{16}\text{O}_{2}$. Each $\text{-COOH}$ to $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ needs 4[H] and loses one O as $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. For two groups: $$\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{4} + 8[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{16}\text{O}_{2} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$

hints: Recall which powerful hydride reagent reduces carboxylic acids all the way to primary alcohols, since milder reagents cannot do this.
walkthrough:
Choose the reagent strong enough for COOH**
Carboxylic acids are very resistant to reduction. $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ will not reduce them. You need lithium aluminium hydride, $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$, in dry ether followed by acid work up, to reduce both $\text{-COOH}$ groups in X to $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ groups in Y.
